name: Panthenol

lead: Panthenol is a vitamin B5 derivative found in moisturisers, shampoos, lip care and healing ointments. It is used to hydrate skin, calm irritation and leave skin and hair feeling softer and smoother.

Skin converts it to pantothenic acid, which is used to make coenzyme A, and it binds water as a humectant. Studies and reviews describe hydration and post-procedure wound-healing roles for dexpanthenol; hair-growth claims lack trial support in the sources reviewed.

paras: It is applied in leave-on moisturisers and serums, as an ingredient in conditioners and shampoos, and in ointments such as Bepanthen for dry, irritated or healing skin. It is a routine ingredient in barrier and post-procedure care.
It is generally well tolerated; rare contact dermatitis or allergy has been reported.

angle.text: Panthenol converts to vitamin B5 in the skin and draws water in as a humectant, so it goes into moisturisers, hair products and wound creams. Skin looks softer and calmer, and human data mainly cover hydration and wound healing.

lead: Panthenol is the alcohol analogue of pantothenic acid (vitamin B5). It is converted in the body to pantothenic acid, so it acts as a provitamin; dexpanthenol is the biologically active D form, while cosmetics may use D-panthenol or a racemic DL mixture.[1][2]

It is used in moisturisers, hair products, lip care and wound-care ointments such as Bepanthen.[1] Reviews describe moisturising and post-procedure wound-healing roles for dexpanthenol,[3][4] and it is generally well tolerated, with rare contact allergy.[1]

paras: Panthenol penetrates skin and is converted to pantothenic acid, a component of coenzyme A.[1][2]
Cosmetic uses include moisturisers, hair products and lip balms, where it is described as a humectant that helps reduce water loss.[1][2] Medical uses include wound and skin-irritation ointments.[1]

A 2011 paper in the Journal of Cosmetic Science examined skin moisturising effects of panthenol-based formulations,[3] and a 2020 review covered dexpanthenol for wound healing after medical and cosmetic procedures.[4] A clinical-dermatology review of common cosmeceuticals also discusses it.[5] The wiki has not summarised effect sizes from these papers. Hair-growth claims rest on cell-level rationale in Grokipedia; no hair-loss trial was located.[2]
Wikipedia reports good tolerability, with rare irritation or contact allergy and low acute toxicity in animals.[1]

Registered human trials include comparisons of Bepanthen ointment with petrolatum after laser therapy (NCT03095872),[6] and trials of dexpanthenol in oral mucositis and diabetic foot ulcers. Published reviews cited above summarise human moisturisation and wound-healing studies.[3][4]
